lessons.title: Conventions
lessons.sub: Planes, axes, which segment moves, the pelvic convention
framing: Most confusion in this material is not about anatomy; it is about naming. The same pelvis can be called rotated left or right depending on whose textbook you open. This lesson fixes the vocabulary the rest of the course uses.

The course names the whole pelvis by the direction it faces in the transverse plane (oriented right or left), each hemipelvis by its own forward or backward rotation and anterior or posterior tilt, and every hip motion as either femur-on-pelvis (FA) or pelvis-on-femur (AF). These terms come from the Postural Restoration Institute and are credited on the About page.

Joint motion is named segment-on-segment: the first segment named is the one moving, and the second is the one held fixed. FA is the femur moving on a fixed pelvis (acetabulum); AF is the pelvis moving on a fixed femur. The same rule gives scapula-on-thorax (ST) and thorax-on-scapula (TS), and humerus-on-glenoid (HG) and glenoid-on-humerus (GH).

In standard anatomy, including Neumann, the innominate is the hip bone (ilium, ischium, pubis). This course borrows the word for any bony ring that positions a spinal region: the pelvic ring (lumbar), the rib cage ring (thoracic), and the cranium and mandible (cervical). This is course usage, not textbook usage.

lessons.title: Landmarks
lessons.sub: Hip bone, sacrum, femur, rib cage, lumbar and thoracic spine
framing: The muscles in this course attach to a small set of bony landmarks on the pelvis, femur, spine, rib cage, and scapula. Before naming attachments in Lesson 4, confirm which bone carries each landmark.
Pick the bone for each landmark. The Lesson 4 attachment list uses these same landmarks.

lessons.title: Visceral anatomy
lessons.sub: Which side the lateralized organs sit on
framing: The thoracic and abdominal cavities are not mirror images. Unit 1 begins from the sides and levels of the major organs, so this lesson asks you to state them once.

It asks only where the organs are. What that asymmetry does, if anything, to posture and gait is a question for Unit 1. Side answers refer to where the greater part of the organ lies relative to the midline in the anatomical position.

lessons.title: Attachments
lessons.sub: Attachments of 23 muscles, in Neumann's terms
framing: For each muscle, choose its attachments from the list. The lesson uses Neumann's terms: proximal and distal for hip and shoulder muscles; inferior and superior for the diaphragm, erector spinae, rectus abdominis, and quadratus lumborum; lateral and medial for the obliques and transversus abdominis. Where a muscle has several attachments at one end, any one of them is accepted.

The muscles are in seven sections: diaphragm and trunk; anterior hip; hamstrings; adductors; gluteal muscles and deep rotators; abdominal wall; and shoulder. Each section's list holds only the attachment sites on the segments those muscles attach to, and each section has its own Check button. The lesson passes when all seven sections are correct.
Fiber distinctions the course uses are listed as separate rows: diaphragm crural vs costal, adductor magnus anterior vs posterior head, and gluteus maximus upper vs lower fibers.

lessons.title: Distal-on-proximal actions
lessons.sub: Femur-on-pelvis, thorax-on-pelvis, scapula-on-thorax, and humerus-on-glenoid, with fiber distinctions
framing: Give each muscle's action in each plane, from anatomical position, with the first-named segment moving: the femur on a fixed pelvis for hip muscles (FA), the thorax on a fixed pelvis for trunk muscles, the scapula on the thorax for scapular muscles (ST), and the humerus on the glenoid for latissimus dorsi (HG).

Trunk muscles are asked the way Neumann's Table 10.3 presents them: one answer for the action with both sides contracting, and one for the action with one side contracting. A one-sided action can combine lateral flexion and rotation; choose the option that names both.

The muscles are in six sections: anterior hip, posterior thigh, medial thigh, gluteal region, trunk, and shoulder. Each section has its own Check button, and the lesson passes when all six sections are correct. The shoulder section has two tables because the moving segment differs: the scapula on the thorax (ST) for the scapular muscles, the humerus on the glenoid (HG) for latissimus dorsi.

Choose None where a muscle has no meaningful action in that plane. Some actions reverse with hip position (piriformis, adductor longus); answer for anatomical position. Lesson 6 asks the same muscles with the roles swapped: the proximal segment moving on a fixed distal one.

lessons.title: Proximal-on-distal actions
framing: Lesson 5 asked what each muscle does when the distal segment moves. This lesson fixes that segment and asks what the same muscle does to the proximal one: the pelvis on a fixed femur (AF), the pelvis on a fixed thorax, the thorax on a fixed scapula (TS), and the trunk on a fixed humerus (GH).

Hip muscles. Neumann describes every hip motion from both perspectives, femoral-on-pelvic and pelvic-on-femoral (Ch. 12, pp. 493-497). Work out which pelvic motion corresponds to each femoral motion, then apply it to the actions Table 12.3 lists for the muscle. Answer from anatomical position, for the side of the fixed femur, and choose None where the table lists no action in that plane. Sagittal answers name the tilt of that hemipelvis; frontal answers say whether the opposite side of the pelvis is raised or lowered; transverse answers say whether the whole pelvis becomes oriented toward or away from the side of the fixed femur.

PRI calls the part of adductor magnus that runs from the ischial tuberosity to the adductor tubercle, above the medial femoral condyle, the ischiocondylar (IC) adductor. Neumann calls the same fibers the posterior, or extensor, head. This lesson uses Neumann's name in its tables.

Trunk muscles. With the thorax held still, a muscle that attaches to both the thorax and the pelvis moves the pelvis (Ch. 10, p. 395). Each trunk muscle has one answer for both sides contracting. Quadratus lumborum also has an answer for one side contracting; the other cells in that column are blank because Neumann does not list a one-sided action on the pelvis for those muscles.

Shoulder muscles. With the scapula or the humerus held still, as when the arms bear weight, these muscles move the thorax and pelvis instead of the limb. The scapular muscles and latissimus dorsi have separate tables because the fixed segment differs.

The answers follow Neumann. Where the clinical model the course draws on (PRI) credits a muscle with a pelvic or rib cage action the text does not list, the course says so in Unit 3; this lesson grades the text. Each section has its own Check button, and the lesson passes when all six sections are correct.

lessons.title: The diaphragm
lessons.sub: Attachments, crural vs costal, zone of apposition
framing: Lesson 4 placed the diaphragm's attachments. This lesson treats it as a muscle: its three parts, what its contraction does to the thorax and the lower ribs, and what has to hold still for it to work.
The first twelve items are textbook anatomy and mechanics from Neumann, Ch. 11. One of them asks about muscles that hold the lower ribs still so the diaphragm can work.

The last two items come from the research literature. The zone of apposition is a described anatomical region, and postural activation of the diaphragm is a measured finding. What a particular rib cage or pelvic position does to either one is a clinical model the course takes up in Unit 1, where it is labeled as model.

lessons.title: Gait phase chart
lessons.sub: Eight Rancho Los Amigos phases, one per screen
framing: This lesson builds a gait chart for one full cycle of the right limb, from right initial contact to the next right initial contact. There is one screen per phase, using the eight periods of the gait cycle in Perry and Burnfield's terminology (the Rancho Los Amigos names). Each phase heading gives its share of the cycle.

Positions are asked at the end of each phase; for initial contact, at the moment of contact. Read them from the kinematic curves in Neumann, Ch. 15, at the percentage where the phase ends. Where a curve sits close to neutral at that point, the neutral option is the answer.

The pelvis is named in the course convention. In the frontal plane, say whether the left side of the pelvis is lower or higher than the right. In the transverse plane, name the direction the whole pelvis faces: when the right side of the pelvis is forward of the left, the pelvis is oriented left. Neumann describes the same motion as rotation of the pelvis about the stance hip.

Each screen is one moment for the whole body, so it also charts the left side. The left limb runs half a cycle behind the right: name the phase the left limb is in, and give the left hip's position in each plane by reading the same curves 50% of the cycle later. Stance is longer than swing, so some screens span two left-limb phases; either is accepted there.
Screens 5 to 8 are screens 1 to 4 with the sides exchanged. Use that to check your chart against itself: the pelvis, the arms, and the two hips should mirror.

Muscle rows ask whether the muscle is active through the phase, for part of it, or not at all, from the timing bars in Neumann's Fig. 15.29. The upper body rows ask which way the shoulder girdle faces and which arm is forward.
Each phase has its own Check button. The lesson passes when all eight phases are correct. Lesson 9 reads directly from this chart.

lessons.title: Pattern-to-phase map
lessons.sub: Read a resting pattern as a moment of walking, then test the muscles against it
framing: This lesson uses the two tables you have built. The first six items read a resting posture against your Lesson 8 gait chart. The last eleven take muscles from your Lesson 6 table and ask how each relates to the pattern.

The pattern is the Left AIC as PRI describes it and as Lesson 1 defined it: pelvis oriented right, left hemipelvis forward and anteriorly tilted, right hemipelvis backward and posteriorly tilted. PRI describes it as the body resting in right stance and left swing. On Neumann's gait data the pelvis is oriented right from the end of right terminal stance, and your chart will show that. That a resting body holds a position from walking is a clinical model, not an established finding; one item asks you to say so.

PRI groups muscles into chains that hold a pattern and muscles of opposition that move the body out of it. For the Left AIC, the anterior interior chain includes the psoas, iliacus, tensor fasciae latae, and biceps femoris. The muscles of opposition are the hamstrings, the gluteals, and the internal obliques, and the course adds the left ischiocondylar adductor. The gluteals are specific by side: the anterior fibers of the left gluteus medius, and on the right the gluteus maximus and the posterior fibers of gluteus medius. The groupings are PRI's and are credited on the About page.

PRI calls the part of adductor magnus that runs from the ischial tuberosity to the adductor tubercle, above the medial femoral condyle, the ischiocondylar (IC) adductor. Neumann calls the same fibers the posterior, or extensor, head.

For each muscle the fixed segment is named. Find the muscle's actions in your Lesson 6 table and choose the one that does what PRI's grouping says: holds the pelvis in the pattern, or moves it out. Each answer is an action Neumann lists. A muscle can have a second listed action that works the other way; Unit 3 takes those up.

lessons.title: Synthesis
lessons.sub: Three short written answers, read by the instructors
framing: Three short written answers, each at least 60 words. They are not auto-graded: both instructors read them before Unit 1, and Unit 1 starts from what the class wrote.
Write from your own chart and tables. Use the course's terms for the pelvis and hip, and say where you are stating a measured fact and where you are stating the model.

where.label: Your Field Atlas pages from Lessons 1 to 9

prompts.text: Describe the moment of walking that the Left AIC pattern resembles. Give the orientation of the pelvis, the position of each hemipelvis, the position of each hip, and which arm is forward.

Name the muscles that would move the body out of that position and into the opposite one (left stance, right swing). For at least three of them, name the fixed segment and the pelvic motion the muscle produces.

Explain why a body might come to rest in that position instead of alternating evenly. Use the course's three premises, and say which parts of your explanation are supported by evidence and which are model.
